scope: Saved-pool final refinement on C150/C192/C208; no root search, SOPT, or independent pipeline scoring. Profiling only: no algorithm/default changes.

fixtures.scaling_selection: First 256 rows of the same C150 source pool; actual distinct candidates, not replicated 16-row input.

findings: Main measured opportunity: reduce repeated CUDA device selection / submission round trips. The 48-candidate trace has 1103 cudaSetDevice calls taking 97.7 ms summed across workers; the 256-candidate trace has 5819 taking 545.6 ms. These overlapping elapsed totals are not predicted wall-time savings.

Murphy GPU evaluation dominates worker elapsed time. Numerical host work is comparatively small: for 48 candidates canonical alpha 20.7 ms, size canonicalization 3.0 ms, search input preparation 9.85 ms (including most coefficient conversions), summed across two workers.
Device transfer activity is only 1.15 ms for 48 candidates. cudaMemcpyAsync API elapsed time includes waiting for GPU computation and driver serialization; it is not transfer bandwidth time.

GPU activity occupies about 264 of 395 ms in the warm 48-candidate trace, and 1195 of 1738 ms in the 256-candidate trace. About 102 / 516 ms respectively has at least one evaluator active but no recorded device kernel/copy activity. This includes host/runtime work and waits, not a proven removable delay.

GPU size preparation is followed by host canonicalization. Its 35.7 ms per three small jobs drops to 15.9 ms for one 256-candidate job: removing redundant GPU size work is especially relevant to tiny replay pools; do not extrapolate the small-pool fraction to 4096 candidates.
Saved-pool replay still builds projective sieve tables: 21.7 ms for the three small jobs, 4.0 ms for the C150 256-candidate job. Consider skipping only when the replay/trace path does not need them.

Single sweep worker medians: 1=0.375, 2=0.393, 4=0.383, 8=0.382 seconds per 48 candidates. More workers did not help here; differences are small enough that defaults should not change on this evidence.
next_steps: First experiment: bind each OpenMP worker to its CUDA device once at job/worker setup, preserving correct device/thread ownership, retries and fallback semantics; compare exact exports and repeat these timings.
Then investigate reducing submission/wait round trips across candidates. Profile the kernel separately if device execution becomes the limiting cost. Keep CPU canonicalization and alpha audits.

Small separate overhead candidates: omit replay-only unused projective tables and avoid GPU size search whose result is replaced by canonical host size. Preserve checked paths and validate representative larger pools.
Re-profile after each measured change; these saved-pool results do not quantify end-to-end pipeline speedup.
